questions.text:
At a campus cafe, 60% of customers order coffee and 40% order tea. Of those who order coffee, 35% also buy a muffin. Of those who order tea, 20% also buy a muffin.

Draw a tree diagram showing all possible outcomes and their probabilities. Use the tree diagram to calculate the probability that a randomly selected student buys a muffin.
questions.expectedAnswer: P(muffin) = P(coffee and muffin) + P(tea and muffin) = 0.60 × 0.35 + 0.40 × 0.20 = 0.21 + 0.08 = 0.29
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Draws tree diagram with correct branches (coffee 0.60/tea 0.40, then muffin/no muffin for each).
- Calculates P(muffin) = 0.29.

For Merit:
- All probabilities correctly labelled on tree with clear working.

For Excellence:
- Fully communicated solution with tree diagram.

questions.text: Given that a student bought a muffin, what is the probability that they ordered coffee? Show your working clearly.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Identifies the need for conditional probability.

For Merit:
- Correctly applies P(coffee|muffin) = P(coffee and muffin)/P(muffin) = 0.21/0.29 = 0.724 (or 21/29).

For Excellence:
- Shows clear reasoning with formula stated, all values identified from the tree.

questions.text:
A prize draw at a community fair costs $5 per ticket. The table below shows the prize structure and probabilities.

Calculate the expected value of the net gain (winnings minus cost) for a single prize draw ticket.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Sets up the expected value calculation correctly with at least 3 of 5 terms.

For Merit:
- Correctly calculates expected winnings = $5.45 and net gain = $0.45.

For Excellence:
- Correctly calculates and interprets — on average a player gains 45 cents per ticket, so the prize draw slightly favours the player.
- the school would need to adjust prize amounts or cost to make it profitable as a fundraiser.

questions.text:
The school wants to make a profit of at least $200 from the prize draw. They expect to sell 400 tickets.

By how much should they increase the cost per ticket so that their expected profit is at least $200? Show your working.
questions.expectedAnswer: Currently expected loss per ticket = -$0.45 (school loses 45c per player). For 400 tickets, need profit ≥ $200, so profit per ticket ≥ $200/400 = $0.50. Current loss per ticket = $0.45. Need to increase cost by $0.45 + $0.50 = $0.95. New cost = $5.95, so the school should increase the ticket price by at least $0.95 to $5.95 (or round up to $6).
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Recognises that the school currently loses money per ticket and attempts to find the required increase.

For Merit:
- Correctly calculates that the cost needs to increase by $0.95 (to $5.95) so expected profit per ticket = $0.50, giving $200 over 400 tickets.

For Excellence:
- Full solution with clear working and verification.

questions.text:
The two-way table below shows survey results from 180 adults about exercise habits and energy levels during the morning.

Calculate the probability that a randomly selected person has high energy, given that they exercise regularly.
questions.markingGuide: Achieved: Correctly identifies the conditional probability and calculates 63/90 = 0.70 (or 7/10).

questions.text:
A fitness company claims: 'Regular exercise boosts your energy — our research shows 70% of regular exercisers have high energy compared to only 27% of those who rarely exercise.'

Evaluate this claim. In your answer, discuss:
• the validity of the comparison
• whether the data supports a causal claim
• what other factors might explain the difference.
questions.expectedAnswer: The comparison is valid — there is a clear difference (70% vs 26.7%). However, the claim of causation is not justified from this observational survey data. Correlation does not imply causation. Confounding variables could explain the difference: people who exercise regularly may also have healthier overall lifestyles, better sleep habits, less stress, different occupations, or different ages. A randomised controlled experiment would be needed to establish causation. The fitness company also has a financial interest in promoting exercise.
questions.markingGuide:
WHAT YOU NEED TO INCLUDE:

For Achievement:
- Notes there is a difference in proportions between the two groups.

For Merit:
- Correctly identifies that this is observational data so causation cannot be concluded, and suggests at least one confounding variable.

For Excellence:
- Thoroughly discusses the limitation of observational studies, provides multiple plausible confounding variables in context, mentions the company's commercial interest, and explains what type of study design would be needed to establish causation.
